episodes.title: Contract WS01 · Contract formation
recap: Shop displays and ordinary adverts are invitations to treat, so the customer makes the offer; only a unilateral advert, like a reward, is an offer.
A reply that changes the terms is a counter-offer and destroys the offer; a mere question leaves it open.
A posted acceptance takes effect on posting, unless the offer requires actual receipt, post is unreasonable or the letter is misaddressed; a revocation takes effect only on receipt.

An offer can be revoked any time before acceptance, even if promised open, unless the offeree gave consideration or has started to perform a unilateral offer; the performer must have known of the offer, and motive does not matter.
A vague key term, or an essential term left to be agreed with no machinery, means no contract; a meaningless subsidiary term is severed, and silence on price gets a reasonable price.
A lock-out binds only if it is for a definite period and supported by consideration; a promise to negotiate in good faith is unenforceable.

episodes.title: DR WS06 · Disclosure and privilege
recap: Regime: intermediate and multi-track claims without personal injury get a disclosure report, then the menu, while fast track and personal injury claims get whatever the court directs, for example standard disclosure.
Disclose and list: an adverse document must always be listed, harm to your case is never a ground to withhold, and the duty to preserve starts once litigation is contemplated.
Inspection: privilege or disproportionality can stop only inspection, a privileged document is still listed, and relying on its contents waives privilege while a mere mention does not.

Missing documents: never listed means specific disclosure, listed but inspection refused as disproportionate means specific inspection, and in pre-action and non-party disclosure the respondent generally gets its costs even though it loses.
Settlement: without prejudice offers are never shown on liability, and only offers marked save as to costs, and Part 36 offers, count on costs.

episodes.title: PP WS06 · Part 2 of 2 · From grant to surrender
recap: Over 3 years needs a deed, 3 years or less skips it only if it is in possession, at the best rent reasonably obtainable, with no premium, and 7 years is only the registration line.

On an open contract the tenant cannot call for the freehold title unless the grant triggers compulsory first registration, but under the Standard Conditions the landlord must deduce title enabling absolute title on a lease over 7 years.

Contracting out needs a simple declaration if the warning notice is at least 14 days before the tenant is bound and a statutory declaration if less, and the tenant is bound by the lease or the agreement for lease, whichever comes first.

A variation without the guarantor's consent releases the guarantor unless it is plainly insubstantial or the guarantee preserves liability, and repair damages are capped at the loss to the reversion, not the cost of the works.
Keys alone are not a surrender, because the landlord must accept unequivocally.

episodes.title: Contract WS06 · Misrepresentation and remedies
recap: One, the statement: a false statement of fact or law made before or at the contract; opinion, intention and silence count only in the narrow cases.
Two, inducement: the statement was material and relied on; not knowing of it, knowing it was untrue or relying on your own investigation defeats that, but a failure to check never does.
Three, the type: fraud needs proven dishonesty or recklessness; under section two-one the maker must prove reasonable grounds and belief up to the contract, so honesty alone is not enough.
Four, undoing it: the contract is voidable, not void, and affirmation, lapse of time, third-party rights or impossible restitution bar rescission.
Five, the money: fraud and section two-one use the tort measure and cover all direct loss; a wholly innocent misrepresentation gets only section two-two damages in lieu or an indemnity.

episodes.summary: A misrepresentation claim runs five questions in order: false statement of fact, inducement, fraud or negligent or innocent, whether rescission is barred, then money, and remember honesty defeats only fraud.

episodes.title: Contract WS07 · Mistake and Privity
recap: Is there a contract at all? An operative mistake makes it void from the start, so nobody is bound and no title passes, and a mistake about value or quality alone isn't enough.

Is the claimant a party? Only a party can enforce, unless the 1999 Act applies, and then a term purporting to benefit an identified third party is enforceable unless the parties did not intend it, and silence does not rebut that.
Is there another route? Agency, assignment, a collateral contract, a trust, tort or statute, and otherwise only the promisee can sue, for its own loss, and the third party's loss only exceptionally.
Does illegality bar the claim? Only if enforcing would harm the integrity of the legal system, weighing purpose, other policy and proportionality, and not the old reliance test.

Is it a restraint of trade? Then it's void unless the party relying on it shows a legitimate interest and that it's no wider than reasonably necessary, and it mustn't be contrary to the public interest.

episodes.summary: First ask whether a mistake makes the contract void, then whether the claimant is a party, is covered by the 1999 Act or has another route, then whether illegality or restraint of trade stands in the way.

episodes.title: CLP WS07 · Hearsay and witnesses
recap: Hearsay only if relied on for the truth of what it states; words used only to show they were said are original evidence.
Four routes in: statute, preserved common law, all parties agree, or interests of justice; abroad or missing counts only if attendance is not reasonably practicable or reasonable steps failed.
Section 126 refuses admission, section 125 stops a jury trial when unconvincing hearsay would make a conviction unsafe, and section 78 PACE covers prosecution evidence only.

Competence needs only understanding questions and giving understandable answers; sworn also needs age 14 and the solemnity of the oath; a spouse is compellable for the prosecution only for a specified offence.

Leading is allowed in cross-examination but not in chief or re-examination except on matters not in dispute; a hostile witness shows no desire to tell the truth and needs the judge's leave, otherwise she is only unfavourable.

episodes.title: Contract WS09 · Damages and Remoteness
recap: Measure the loss: damages compensate and never punish, expectation is the default, and with a market for the goods it is the market price on the due date.
Cause: the breach has to be an effective cause, not merely the opportunity for the loss.
Remoteness: loss that arises naturally, or from special circumstances the defendant actually knew at contracting, and once the type of loss was a serious possibility the full extent is recoverable.
Cutting it down: the defendant has to prove the claimant missed reasonable steps, and only a benefit caused by the breach gets deducted.

Money back: a total failure of consideration returns the whole payment, a partial failure only if it can be apportioned, and a reasonable true deposit is forfeited, with 10 per cent the conventional deposit for land.
Consumers: 30 days to reject, then one repair or replacement, then price reduction or final rejection, and there is no right to reject a service.

episodes.title: Contract WS08 · Breach and Frustration
recap: Did it end with no breach? A termination clause's specified event is enough, if you operate it strictly.
Does the breach let you terminate? Only a condition, a serious innominate breach, a renunciation or disabling yourself does, and terminate without that right and you're the one in breach.
Accept or affirm? A breach ends nothing until the innocent party accepts it, and affirming knowingly leaves damages for that breach, not loss of bargain.
Mistake or frustration? Frustration needs an event after the contract, with no fault, making performance impossible, illegal or radically different; more cost is not enough.
Who gets what back? Section one, subsection two covers money paid or payable, with expenses capped at those sums; subsection three values the end product.

Who pays for half-done work? A party in breach of an entire obligation who performed only partly gets nothing, unless the other side freely chose to accept it; accepting goods ends the right to reject.

episodes.summary: Ask whether it ended without breach, then whether the breach was repudiatory; the innocent party chooses, terminate without the right and you're the one in breach, and frustration needs a no-fault event making performance impossible, illegal or radically different.

episodes.title: Contract WS10 · Penalties and Equitable Remedies
recap: A valid agreed sum is paid without proof of loss, and no more; it is a penalty only if triggered by breach and out of all proportion to a legitimate interest.
Specific performance only where damages are inadequate, and specific goods are not enough if they can be bought on the market.
A clear negative promise is ordinarily enforced by injunction without asking if damages are adequate, even in personal services if it does not in effect compel work.
Indemnity or guarantee is decided by substance: liable only if another defaults means a guarantee.
A guarantee needs signed writing, consideration or a deed, a valid principal obligation, and a default.

A material variation without the guarantor's consent discharges the guarantor unless it is plainly insubstantial or incapable of prejudicing them. A binding agreement for extra time or release of the debtor also discharges the guarantor, and lost security discharges to the extent of the loss, but a clear preserving clause keeps the guarantor liable despite variations and indulgences.

episodes.title: BLP WS07 · Corporation Tax and VAT
recap: Corporation tax: a UK resident company pays on total profits for each accounting period of up to 12 months; the limits shrink for associated companies and short periods; pay 9 months and 1 day after the period, or by instalments if large.

Income profits: income expenditure wholly and exclusively for the trade comes off, including salaries, employer's NICs, employer pension contributions and business interest; dividends paid, depreciation, client entertainment and capital expenditure do not; full expensing is a full first-year allowance for companies on new and unused main-rate plant.

Gains: a company's gains are total profits, with indexation only up to December 2017 and no annual exempt amount, BADR or gift relief; the SSE exempts a gain on at least 10% of a trading company held for a continuous 12 months within the 6 years before disposal.

Rollover relief: it defers the gain, by deduction from the new asset's base cost, when the proceeds are reinvested in a qualifying asset from 1 year before to 3 years after; if only part is reinvested, the gain is chargeable at once up to the proceeds not reinvested; a company cannot claim for goodwill.
Loss relief: same period, then the previous 12 months only after a current-period claim, then forward; only a cessation opens the 3-year terminal carry-back; capital losses stay with gains.

Close companies: a UK resident company controlled by 5 or fewer participators, or participator-directors, with more than 50% control; a loan brings a refundable charge on the company unless an exception applies; a benefit to a non-working participator is a distribution; phoenixism needs at least 5%, a similar trade within 2 years and a main purpose.

VAT scope: five conditions; registration counts taxable supplies only; the historic test notifies within 30 days of the month end, the future test by the end of the 30 days; an exempt-only supplier cannot register.

VAT charging: silence means VAT-inclusive; a later invoice moves the tax point only within 14 days; zero-rated is taxable, exempt is not; return and payment by 1 month and 7 days after the period; only cash accounting, or the flat rate scheme's cash-based method, follows payment.

Distributions: interest is deductible, dividends are not; a buyback payment above the capital subscribed is income unless all six conditions or the IHT route are met; a liquidator's payment is capital, subject to the winding-up anti-avoidance rule.
Anti-avoidance: evasion is a crime and must be refused; the GAAR needs an abusive tax arrangement and does not cover VAT; a salaried member needs all of A, B and C.

recap: No expert evidence without the court's permission, which covers only the named field or expert; the small claims, fast and intermediate tracks limit it further.

episodes.title: Tort WS04 · Remoteness, defences and remedies
recap: Remoteness: D is liable for the reasonably foreseeable kind of harm, judged at the time of breach and usually described broadly, however it happened and however bad it was.
Consent: a complete defence, but it normally fails for an employee who merely knew of the danger, a rescuer under a duty and the very act, and always for a car passenger.
Contributory negligence: a partial defence, never 100 per cent, with standard figures for seatbelts and helmets that depend on how much difference the belt or helmet would have made.
Illegality: a complete defence; an incidental crime does not bar the claim, but injury that is a foreseeable risk of a joint criminal enterprise is barred.
Remedies: restore the pre-tort position, normally as one lump sum, and C must mitigate.
Personal injury damages: special and general damages, Ogden multipliers for continuing future loss, and no recovery for a defendant's unpaid care.
Deductions: benefits come off like for like and never off PSLA; own accident insurance, ill-health or disability pensions and charitable payments or gifts stay.

Claims on death: the estate's losses up to death, listed dependants' lost reasonable expectation of financial benefit where the deceased could have sued, and a fixed bereavement award for a few people only.

episodes.title: PP WS07 · Lease structure and content
recap: An agreement for lease is a land contract, in writing, with all terms, signed by both; a lease needs a deed unless it is up to 3 years, in possession, at best rent and with no premium; a variation is a new lease only if it extends the term or adds premises.
Context only, not a rule: void periods, market changes and management costs put a landlord's income at risk.

The tenant pays SDLT, or LTT in Wales, on the grant; the return and tax are due within 14 days of the effective date for SDLT, or 30 days for LTT; first-time buyer relief exists for SDLT only, and only if the lease has at least 21 years to run.

A lease must be registered if possession starts more than 3 months after grant, whatever its length, or if it is over 7 years; leases of 3 years or less override and cannot be noted; an unregistered registrable lease is only equitable.

Alterations turn on the covenant: none, absolute, qualified, or fully qualified; a qualified covenant becomes reasonable only for an improvement judged from the tenant's view, and the landlord may still ask a reasonable sum for loss and, for an improvement not adding letting value, require reinstatement where reasonable.

Section 3 lets a business tenant improve despite the lease: notice, 3 months to object, and if the landlord objects, a court certificate, which needs added letting value; if the landlord offers to do the works itself for a reasonable rent increase, the court cannot certify and the tenant need not accept.

A qualified user covenant is never made reasonable by statute; the landlord may refuse but, unless structural alterations are involved, may not charge a fine or a rent increase for consent; only some covenants are upgraded by statute.

Works or a change of use may need planning permission, which the lease and any licence make the tenant obtain; the Code is good practice, now a RICS standard whose mandatory parts bind only RICS members and regulated firms.

episodes.title: CLP WS08 · Sentencing (part 1 of 2)
recap: Sources and purposes of sentencing: no checked point is taught yet; the duty to follow guidelines comes under the guidelines topic.
Which court sentences: if the magistrates consider their powers inadequate for an either-way offence, they may commit for sentence, and the Crown Court can then go up to the offence's maximum.

Basis of plea: where the prosecution does not accept D's basis and the difference would materially affect sentence, the court sentences on D's version or holds a Newton hearing, unless D's version is absurd or obviously untenable; the prosecution proves its version beyond reasonable doubt; a Newton hearing cannot decide an element of the offence.

Totality: concurrent is ordinarily right for one incident or a series of the same kind, especially against the same person, unless that would not reflect the overall criminality; consecutive is normally right for unrelated or distinct offences, a same-kind series that concurrent terms would not reflect (eg different victims), or to avoid undermining a statutory minimum; either way the overall sentence must be just and proportionate.
Deferring sentence: no checked point is taught yet.

Indications of sentence: in the magistrates' court, once D indicates a guilty plea after an indication, no court may impose custody unless custody was indicated, subject to a limited exception, and otherwise the indication binds no court; the Crown Court indication is not covered here.

Seriousness is culpability plus harm caused, intended or foreseeably possible; custody needs an offence so serious that neither a fine alone nor a community sentence can be justified, and a community order needs an imprisonable offence serious enough to warrant it.

Guidelines: every court must follow a relevant guideline unless that would be contrary to the interests of justice; in the stepped approach any assistance reduction comes before the guilty plea reduction.

The sentencing hearing: the defence speaks last; before deciding the thresholds, the length of custody or the requirements, a pre-sentence report must be obtained unless the court considers it unnecessary, and for under 18s it can be unnecessary only if there is an existing report; D must prove a mitigating fact the prosecution cannot be expected to know, on the balance of probabilities; reasons are given in open court.
Aggravating and mitigating factors: only some are statutory; the rest come from guidelines, and provocation mitigates only where an offence-specific guideline lists it.

Credit for a guilty plea: maximum one-third at the first stage, one-quarter after unless particular circumstances made an earlier plea unreasonable, down to one-tenth on the first day of trial; for murder one-sixth and never more than 5 years; exceptions for a rejected Newton version and for minimum sentences.

recap: Discharges and bind overs: nothing is checked on them yet, so nothing is taught here.
Fines: nothing is checked on fines themselves yet; a fine can be imposed alongside a community order and is an option on breach.

Community orders and requirements: available only for an offender aged 18 or over convicted of an imprisonable offence that is serious enough to warrant one; at least one requirement and up to 3 years; the requirements must be the most suitable and commensurate with seriousness, with at least one punitive requirement unless a fine is also imposed or exceptional circumstances apply; three requirements need the offender's consent.

Breach of a community order: the officer must warn or refer, and must refer if a warning was given within the previous 12 months; on proof the court must amend, fine up to £2,500, or revoke and re-sentence; a further offence is not a breach of the requirements.

Custodial sentences: not unless so serious that neither a fine alone nor a community sentence can be justified, subject to exceptions; the shortest term commensurate with seriousness, subject to exceptions; automatic release on licence at the halfway point, or 40 per cent for most standard determinate sentences, with exclusions, and two-thirds for specified serious offences with long sentences; remand time counts automatically and a qualifying tagged curfew counts half a day for each day.

Suspended sentence orders: a custodial sentence, so the threshold and shortest term come first; for an adult convicted on or after 22 March 2026, where an order is available, a term of 12 months or less must be suspended unless exceptional circumstances or an exclusion applies, and otherwise the ordinary power remains; breach means activation unless unjust.

Minimum sentences: set by offence group and age; the drug trafficking, burglary and weapon minimums apply, for offences on or after 28 June 2022, unless exceptional circumstances relating to the offence or offender justify not imposing them (earlier offences: unless particular circumstances make it unjust); the firearms minimum applies unless exceptional circumstances justify not imposing it.

Extended determinate sentences: for an offender aged 21 or over, a specified offence and a significant risk of serious harm are not enough; the court also needs a qualifying previous conviction or a long enough custodial term.
Life sentences: for an offender aged 21 or over, a listed offence meeting the dangerousness test means life must be imposed if the seriousness justifies it.
Professional conduct at sentencing: no duty to reveal previous convictions the prosecution has not revealed, but never mislead the court, whether by stating or by implying there are none.

episodes.title: Dispute Resolution WS08 · ADR and discontinuance (part 1 of 2)
recap: Types of ADR: arbitrators, expert determination and construction adjudication decide; mediators and conciliators only help the parties settle, and a mediation binds only if they reach agreement.
Why use ADR: mediation suits a continuing relationship, confidentiality or an outcome a court cannot order, but only litigation gives the court's coercive powers, and ADR is not always cheaper.
The lawyer's role: explain the options with their cost and risk, settle only within instructions, and remember mediation can happen at any time, before or during proceedings.
The court and ADR: the court can order ADR if the order is proportionate, and an unreasonable refusal can cost a party even if it wins, with the burden on the unsuccessful party to show it.

Discontinuance: usually no permission is needed, except in three cases, and unless the court orders otherwise the claimant pays the defendant's costs up to service of the notice, though not on the small claims track.

episodes.title: Dispute Resolution WS08 · Part 36 offers (part 2 of 2)
recap: Nature: a Part 36 offer can be made at any time, survives rejection and can be accepted until withdrawn, whereas a Calderbank offer is only weighed in the costs discretion; the trial orders are not automatic, because the court must make them unless it considers it unjust.

Valid offer: it must meet every form requirement, including a relevant period of not less than 21 days unless it is made less than 21 days before trial, otherwise it has none of the Part 36 consequences.

Withdrawing: a notice served during the relevant period takes effect only at its end if the offer has not been accepted, and an acceptance before then stands unless the offeror applies in time and the court finds a change of circumstances.

Accepting: an offer can be accepted until withdrawn, with the court's permission in some cases, and accepting after the relevant period normally costs the claimant the costs from expiry unless the court considers that unjust.

At trial: the claimant must fail to beat a defendant's offer, or do at least as well as its own, and then the court must make the orders unless it considers it unjust, but never for a withdrawn offer, a worsened offer the offeree beat, or an offer made less than 21 days before trial unless the court abridged the period.

episodes.title: CLP WS08 · Sentencing (part 1 of 2)
recap: Sources and purposes of sentencing: no checked point is taught yet; the duty to follow guidelines comes under the guidelines topic.
Which court sentences: if the magistrates consider their powers inadequate for an either-way offence, they may commit for sentence, and the Crown Court can then go up to the offence's maximum.

Basis of plea: where the prosecution does not accept D's basis and the difference would materially affect sentence, the court sentences on D's version or holds a Newton hearing, unless D's version is absurd or obviously untenable; the prosecution proves its version beyond reasonable doubt; a Newton hearing cannot decide an element of the offence.

Totality: concurrent is ordinarily right for one incident or a series of the same kind, especially against the same person, unless that would not reflect the overall criminality; consecutive is normally right for unrelated or distinct offences, a same-kind series that concurrent terms would not reflect (eg different victims, or domestic abuse or sexual offences against the same individual), or to avoid undermining a statutory minimum; either way the overall sentence must be just and proportionate.
Deferring sentence: no checked point is taught yet.

Indications of sentence: in the magistrates' court, once D indicates a guilty plea after an indication, no court may impose custody unless custody was indicated, subject to a limited exception, and otherwise the indication binds no court; in the Crown Court only D may seek a Goodyear indication, normally at the plea and trial preparation hearing and with his signed written authority; the judge may refuse or defer it; once given it binds any judge on the case unless D fails to plead guilty after a reasonable opportunity, though the Attorney General can still refer an unduly lenient sentence where that power arises.

Seriousness is culpability plus harm caused, intended or foreseeably possible; custody needs an offence so serious that neither a fine alone nor a community sentence can be justified, and a community order needs an imprisonable offence serious enough to warrant it.

Guidelines: every court must follow a relevant guideline unless that would be contrary to the interests of justice; in the stepped approach any assistance reduction comes before the guilty plea reduction.

The sentencing hearing: the defence speaks last; before deciding the thresholds, the length of custody or the requirements, a pre-sentence report must be obtained unless the court considers it unnecessary, and for under 18s it can be unnecessary only if there is an existing report; D must prove a mitigating fact the prosecution cannot be expected to know, on the balance of probabilities; reasons are given in open court.
Aggravating and mitigating factors: only some are statutory; the rest come from guidelines, and provocation mitigates only where an offence-specific guideline lists it.

Credit for a guilty plea: maximum one-third at the first stage, one-quarter after unless particular circumstances made an earlier plea unreasonable, down to one-tenth on the first day of trial; for murder one-sixth and never more than 5 years; exceptions for a rejected Newton version and for minimum sentences.

episodes.title: WAE WS08 · Revocation of wills, and forfeiture
recap: Destruction revokes only with an actual act (not a symbolic one) together with the intention to revoke and capacity, and destruction by another person revokes only if done in the testator's presence and at their direction.
A revocation made on an assumption that proves false, when the testator would not otherwise have revoked, does not take effect.
A missing or mutilated will last known to be in the testator's possession is presumed revoked, but rebuttably, and no presumption arises where someone else held it.
A valid later will with a revocation clause revokes all earlier wills and codicils; without one it revokes only what is inconsistent.
A valid codicil executed with the same formalities as a will can revoke the whole or part of a will, expressly or by inconsistency.
Mutual wills and mirror wills: not covered here yet, so use the workshop notes.
Marriage or civil partnership revokes an earlier will, subject to exceptions, including a will made in contemplation of marriage to a particular person.
A final order of divorce or dissolution does not revoke the will but, unless it shows a contrary intention, the former spouse is treated as having died; only a final order counts.

Someone who unlawfully kills the deceased, or unlawfully aids, abets, counsels or procures the death, cannot benefit under the will or on intestacy; the court may modify the rule for any unlawful killing except where the offender stands convicted of murder, only where the justice of the case requires it, and after a conviction only if proceedings are brought within 3 months of it.

episodes.title: Property Practice WS08 · Alienation (part 1 of 2)
recap: An underlease is a new lease shorter than the tenant's own remaining term, at least by one day; a sub-grant of the whole remaining term operates as an assignment.

A qualified covenant against underletting is read as fully qualified, so consent cannot be unreasonably withheld; refusal is reasonable only if it relates to the landlord and tenant relationship in regard to the subject matter of the lease, not a collateral advantage.

With no privity between head landlord and undertenant, the licence to underlet carries a direct covenant; a covenant restricting use in a new head lease can also bind an undertenant, and the head landlord may forfeit the head lease, ending the underlease unless the undertenant obtains relief.

The tenant pays the landlord's reasonable costs, usually under an undertaking, whether or not the deal proceeds; the undertenant should see the head lease, the consent and, ideally, the freehold title.

A lease of more than 7 years granted out of a registered title is registrable; search with priority before completion and apply to register within the priority period; until registered, the tenant holds only an equitable lease.

A licence records consent, conditions and covenants; whether a direct covenant binds an assignee beyond its release depends on whether the lease is old or new, and accepting rent with knowledge of a once-and-for-all breach can waive forfeiture.
After an assignment, notice goes to the landlord within the time the lease requires, with any fee, and the receipt is kept with the deeds.

Qualified covenants against charging and parting with possession are also made fully qualified, but the pre-agreed circumstances rule covers assignment only; the Code for Leasing sets out heads of terms.

episodes.title: Property Practice WS08 · Alienation (part 2 of 2)
recap: Assignment passes the whole remaining term and the assignee becomes the landlord's tenant; a sublease of the whole remaining term operates as an assignment.

A qualified covenant against assignment is fully qualified, and after a written application the landlord must act within a reasonable time and prove any refusal or condition reasonable; only in a non-residential new lease can circumstances and conditions be pre-agreed, and only for assignment.

On an old lease the original tenant stays liable for the whole term; on a new lease the original tenant is released on assigning the whole premises, except for an excluded assignment, earlier breaches and any AGA.
An AGA, lawfully required as a condition of consent, makes the outgoing tenant of a new lease guarantee its immediate assignee only, until that assignee is released.

The buyer inherits the lease and investigates it; absolute leasehold means the superior title need not be investigated, but good leasehold does not protect against rights affecting the landlord's title, and the two sets of standard conditions treat missing consent differently.

The transfer must be by deed and, on the standard conditions, the seller does not warrant the physical state of the property; the buyer searches with priority, pays SDLT on the premium only, and registers within the priority period or the time allowed for first registration.

episodes.title: WAE WS09 · Amending and republishing wills
recap: Choosing the method: a codicil suits a small, simple change; a new will is better for substantial changes.
Incorporated documents, STEP provisions and letters of wishes: a look-up topic, covered in the Quizlet set.

Manuscript alterations: an alteration made after execution has no effect unless executed like a will or validated by a later confirming codicil, but original words made no longer apparent are revoked; unattested alterations are presumed to be made after execution, unless evidence rebuts that.

Exceptions: if the original words are still apparent they stand; if they are not apparent they are revoked, unless they were obliterated only to make way for a new gift that fails for want of execution, when conditional revocation applies and they can be proved by extrinsic evidence.
Codicils: made with the same formalities as a will, and read with it; where inconsistent, the codicil prevails and the rest of the will stands.
Republication: a codicil confirming the will makes it take effect as if executed at the codicil's date, subject to contrary intention.

Revocation and revival: revival needs re-execution or a duly executed codicil showing an intention to revive; revoking the revoking document is not enough, and a destroyed will cannot be revived, although a mistaken destruction may be a conditional revocation that fails.
Recap: destroying part of a will revokes only that part, unless the part destroyed is so important that the rest cannot stand.

episodes.title: CLP WS09 · Summary trial and appeals to the Court of Appeal (part 1 of 2)
recap: First hearings: the parties must actively assist case management, initial details of the prosecution case are due by the beginning of the day of the first hearing, and the magistrates' limits are 6 months for a summary offence and 12 months for an either-way offence.

Not guilty plea: directions are given at that hearing using the PET form and the trial date is fixed, and standard directions usually put the defence statement and defence witness notice within 14 days.

Pre-trial rulings bind until the case is disposed of, unless discharged on sending to the Crown Court or an indictment, or discharged or varied on three conditions, with a party's application needing a material change of circumstances.
Pleading guilty by post: not covered in this episode; take it from the workshop notes.

Burden and standard: the prosecution bears the legal burden and must make the magistrates sure, subject to insanity and statutory exceptions where the defendant carries the burden of a defence on the balance of probabilities.

Trial procedure: the order of trial, written statements read unless another party objects in time, the no case to answer test, and the defendant's choice whether to give evidence with the court making sure he knows the consequences of silence.
Retirement, verdict and reasons: not covered in this episode; take it from the workshop notes.
Crown Court slip rule: not covered in this episode; take it from the workshop notes.
Conviction appeal test: the Court of Appeal must allow the appeal if it thinks the conviction unsafe and must otherwise dismiss it.
Leave and procedure: leave is needed unless the judge certifies within 28 days, the notice is due within 28 days, and a refused applicant can renew within 10 business days.

Grounds: conviction grounds succeed only if they make the conviction unsafe, sentence grounds are manifestly excessive or wrong in principle, and after a guilty plea a conviction appeal needs a vitiated plea or one of the further situations.

Powers: on a successful conviction appeal the court quashes and acquits or orders a retrial, or may substitute an alternative offence with no more severe sentence; on a sentence appeal the defendant must not be dealt with more severely as a whole.
Loss of time: a discretion, with reasons, never available where leave was granted, the judge certified or the Criminal Cases Review Commission referred.
Fresh evidence: received if necessary or expedient in the interests of justice, considering four factors.

Attorney General's references: the Attorney General, not the prosecution, may refer an unduly lenient sentence with leave, within 28 days or the extended 14 days, and the court may pass a more severe sentence.
Criminal Cases Review Commission: not covered in this episode; take it from the workshop notes.
Prosecution appeals and challenging acquittals: not covered in this episode; take it from the workshop notes.
Supreme Court: only if the Court of Appeal certifies a point of law of general public importance and leave is granted by that court or the Supreme Court.

recap: The complaint picks the route: a dispute of fact suits an appeal to the Crown Court, a pure point of law or jurisdiction suits a case stated, which any party may use, and a defendant who applies for a case stated loses his appeal to the Crown Court.

Any party may apply within 21 days to have a case stated on law or jurisdiction; magistrates may refuse only if the application is frivolous and never for the Attorney General; the Divisional Court decides on the facts as stated.

episodes.title: DR WS09 · Appeals and trial preparation (part 1 of 2)
recap: Grounds of appeal and the nature of an appeal: the appeal court allows an appeal where the decision was wrong, or unjust because of a serious procedural or other irregularity; an appeal is normally a review, not a re-hearing, unless a practice direction provides otherwise or the court decides a re-hearing is in the interests of justice.

Permission to appeal and time limits; no automatic stay: permission is needed for appeals from a judge in the County Court or High Court, with exceptions; first appeals need a real prospect of success or another compelling reason, second appeals also an important point of principle or practice or another compelling reason; the appellant's notice is due within 21 days of the decision unless the lower court directs a different period, the parties cannot agree an extension, and an appeal does not stay the order unless a court orders one.

Routes of appeal: for a first appeal the level of the judge decides the destination, subject to limited specialist exceptions; any second appeal goes to the Court of Appeal; the Supreme Court needs permission.

Powers of the appeal court and fresh evidence: the court may affirm, set aside or vary, send back, order a new hearing and make orders on interest and costs; fresh evidence comes in only if it could not have been obtained with reasonable diligence for trial, would probably have had an important influence, and is apparently credible.

Settlement: a consent order or a Tomlin order is a court order, and a Tomlin order's scheduled terms can be enforced in the same proceedings; a settlement agreement not embodied in a court order must be sued on.

Pre-trial checklists and listing directions: the checklist checks readiness near the end, unlike the directions questionnaire; on the fast and intermediate tracks it is filed not more than 8 weeks before trial, and if no party files, the statements of case are struck out unless a completed checklist is filed within 7 days.

Notices to prove documents and witness summonses: a disclosed document's authenticity is deemed admitted unless notice to prove it is served in time; a witness summons requires a witness to attend and/or produce documents.

episodes.title: Contract WS07 · Mistake · Part 1 of 3
recap: An operative mistake makes the contract void from the start, so neither party is bound and no title passes; that is the contrast with misrepresentation, which only makes a contract voidable.

Common mistake as to existence is void unless a party promised the subject matter existed; as to quality it is void only if the shared assumption makes the subject matter or performance essentially and radically different, with no warranty and no fault; unilateral mistake about terms means no contract only if the other party knows or ought to know; about quality it is caveat emptor unless induced by misrepresentation; cross-purposes is decided objectively; non est factum needs a radically different document and no carelessness.

Face to face, a rogue's contract is voidable for fraud, a buyer in good faith and without notice before rescission gets good title, and a vanished rogue is rescinded against by taking all reasonable steps; in writing, a real person impersonated makes the contract void and no title passes.

episodes.title: Contract WS09 · Remedies for breach of contract
recap: Introduction to remedies: every breach is actionable without proof of loss, but with no loss proved the claimant gets nominal damages only.

The assessment of damages: damages are compensatory, never punitive, and start from expectation; cost of cure only if reasonable, reliance for wasted spending (reduced or defeated if the defendant proves it would not have been recouped), and with an available market the market rule applies prima facie, whether or not a substitute deal was made.

Particular types of loss: distress is generally not recoverable, except where pleasure, relaxation or peace of mind was a major or important object of the contract, or physical inconvenience and discomfort was caused; a lost chance that depended on a third party needs a real and substantial chance and is discounted, while the claimant's own hypothetical act is proved on the balance of probabilities.

Causation: the breach must be an effective cause, not merely the opportunity for the loss; a third party's act breaks the chain only if it was not a likely consequence, unless the defendant's duty was to guard against it, and the claimant's own unreasonable conduct breaks it if it is the real cause.

Remoteness: loss must arise in the usual course of things or from special circumstances known to the defendant when the contract was made; only its type need have been a serious possibility, and information given after contracting does not count.

Mitigation: the defendant must prove the claimant failed to take reasonable steps, and only the avoidable loss is irrecoverable; reasonable costs are added, benefits are deducted only if caused by the breach, and there is no duty to mitigate until a repudiation is accepted, or for a debt claim.

Account of profits and negotiating damages: an account of profits is awarded only exceptionally, where other remedies are inadequate and there is a legitimate interest in preventing the profit; negotiating damages need a valuable asset taken by the breach.

Restitution and unjust enrichment: a valid contract's allocation of risk prevails; money paid is recoverable for a total failure of consideration but not, at common law, for a partial failure unless apportionable; a true deposit is forfeited if reasonable, and for land 10% is conventional.

The Achilleas: exceptionally, a loss within the Hadley test is still too remote if the defendant cannot reasonably be taken to have assumed responsibility for that kind of loss; in most cases the standard Hadley test applies without that step.

Consumer remedies for goods: a short-term right to reject within 30 days; after that one repair or replacement, then a price reduction or a final rejection, with no deduction for use within 6 months of delivery except for motor vehicles.
Consumer remedies for digital content: the guide teaches nothing on this topic.

Consumer remedies for services: a service cannot be rejected; repeat performance first, then a price reduction only if that is impossible or not provided; a late service gives a price reduction only, though damages remain available.

episodes.title: BLP WS09 · Insolvency procedures, corporate and personal
recap: A company is deemed unable to pay its debts if a statutory demand for a debt over £750 goes unpaid for 3 weeks, and a debt disputed on substantial grounds is protected by an injunction against the winding-up petition.

Where the company is insolvent or bordering on insolvency, or insolvent liquidation or administration is probable, directors must consider creditors' interests and balance them against members' interests, and once insolvent liquidation or administration is inevitable creditors' interests are paramount; a real but not remote risk of insolvency does not trigger the duty.

A standalone moratorium lasts 20 business days, extendable by the directors for a further 20, up to a year with creditor consent or to any date the court orders, and it is a payment holiday for most pre-moratorium debts, with five exceptions.

A CVA approved by 75% in value of the creditors voting, unless more than 50% of the unconnected creditors vote against, binds every unsecured creditor entitled to vote, but not a secured or preferential creditor's rights without its consent, and it brings no moratorium of its own.

A restructuring plan is voted on class by class at 75% in value of each class voting and needs the court's sanction; it then binds every creditor and member in those classes, secured creditors included, and the court can cram down a dissenting class if none of its members would be worse off than in the relevant alternative and 75% in value of a class with a payment or genuine economic interest in that alternative agreed.

Expenses and preferential debts come out of floating charge assets ahead of the floating chargeholder, never out of fixed charge assets, and a fixed charge creditor's shortfall ranks as unsecured but cannot share in the prescribed part.

An IVA has the same creditor majorities as a CVA, binds unsecured creditors entitled to vote, cannot affect a secured creditor's right to enforce or a preferential creditor's priority without consent, and can have its own moratorium, an interim order.

A creditor may petition for bankruptcy on an unsecured, liquidated, undisputed debt of at least £5,000 unpaid after a statutory demand for 3 weeks, and a spouse's or civil partner's loan is postponed only if she held that status when the bankruptcy began.

Discharge comes after 1 year, but income payments and the trustee's claim to the home can last up to 3 years, and on a trustee's application to sell the home made more than 1 year after vesting the court assumes, unless the circumstances are exceptional, that the creditors' interests outweigh all other considerations.

A transaction at an undervalue is caught within 5 years before the petition, with insolvency shown beyond 2 years unless the recipient is an associate, a preference within 6 months, or 2 years for an associate, and a transaction defrauding creditors has no look-back period and needs no insolvency.

The administrator must aim to rescue the company unless he thinks that is not reasonably practicable or that a better result for creditors as a whole is available, and the notice period before an out-of-court appointment depends on who is appointing.

Proposals are due within 8 weeks and administration ends after 1 year unless extended before it expires, and the moratorium bars winding up and an administrative receiver outright, while consent or permission lifts only the other bars.
A fixed charge receiver acts mainly for the chargee and deals only with the charged asset, and there is no moratorium, so other creditors can still sue.
Liquidation is compulsory by court order or voluntary by special resolution, and it ends in dissolution 3 months after the final account or notice is registered, unless the date is deferred.

Whether the directors make a declaration of solvency within the 5 weeks before the special resolution decides whether the members (MVL) or the creditors (CVL) choose the liquidator, and an MVL becomes a CVL if the liquidator concludes the debts will not be paid in full within the stated period.

Misfeasance proceedings let the liquidator or official receiver recover from officers who misapplied company property or breached their duties, and administration aims first at rescue under a moratorium while liquidation ends the company.

episodes.title: Contract WS06 · Misrepresentation
recap: Elements: an unambiguous, false statement of existing fact or law, made by one party to the other before or at the time of contracting, that induced the contract, and the contract is then voidable, not void.

Opinion and future intention are generally not statements of fact, and silence is generally not a misrepresentation, unless an exception applies: an opinion not honestly held or from a maker better placed to know the facts, an intention not held when stated, or an exception to silence.

Categories: if the claimant cannot prove fraud, the representor is liable in damages under section 2(1) unless it proves reasonable grounds to believe, and actual belief, up to the contract; if it proves both, the misrepresentation is wholly innocent.

Remedies: rescission is open in every category, subject to the bars and, for a non-fraudulent misrepresentation, to the court's discretion to award damages in lieu; fraud and section 2(1) give all direct loss; wholly innocent gives no damages as of right; an exclusion clause must be reasonable, or fair in a consumer contract.
Alternatives: a statement the parties objectively intended to be binding is a term, and a non-party's statement points to Hedley Byrne.

episodes.title: CLP WS10 · Sentencing children (part 1 of 2)
recap: Every court sentencing a child must follow the children guideline unless that would be contrary to the interests of justice; without a children's guideline for the offence, the court may look at the adult guideline but must not apply it mechanically.

A parent or guardian must attend court with a child under 16 unless the court considers that unreasonable; any court sentencing a child, including the Crown Court, may bind over a parent, with the parent's consent and not alongside a referral order.

A detention and training order for a child aged 12 to 14 at conviction, and a youth rehabilitation order with ISS or fostering for a child under 15 at conviction, need a persistent offender; three findings of guilt in the past 12 months for comparable imprisonable offences can certainly justify that label, but one previous offence is not enough.

A youth rehabilitation order with ISS or fostering needs an imprisonable offence and the custody threshold passed, plus persistence only if the child is under 15 at conviction, so a 15-year-old need not be persistent.

A referral order always needs a guilty plea to the offence or a connected offence; it must be made if the compulsory conditions are met (an imprisonable offence, a guilty plea to it and any connected offences, and no previous conviction in the UK), unless the court proposes custody, an absolute discharge, a hospital order or a conditional discharge.

A detention and training order lasts 4 to 24 months, never longer than the adult maximum, and a plea reduction that takes it below 4 months means a non-custodial sentence; custody beyond 24 months is only available in the Crown Court.

episodes.title: CLP WS10 · The youth court and the police station (part 2 of 2)
recap: A youth is aged 10 to 17 inclusive; age at first appearance decides the court, and a defendant who is 18 by then goes to the adult courts, while sentencing powers depend on age at conviction.
Youths are presumed to be tried in the youth court and have no right to elect Crown Court trial, but some appear in the adult magistrates' court.

The youth court must send some cases to the Crown Court, such as homicide; for a grave crime, after a not guilty (or no) plea indication, it should send only if there is a real prospect of long-term detention, in practice more than 2 years, and it must send a specified offence if the extended sentence criteria would be met, which is rarely decided at the first hearing.

A youth charged alongside an adult first appears in the adult magistrates' court. If the adult is sent for trial, the youth goes too under the youth's own sending rules, or if the court considers it necessary in the interests of justice.
After a Crown Court conviction for anything other than homicide, the youth is remitted to the youth court for sentence unless the Crown Court is satisfied that would be undesirable.
Only in the youth court is the press automatically barred from identifying the youth, and youth court trials are not open to the public.
A juvenile needs an appropriate adult, who must be present for an interview or a written statement, save an urgent interview authorised on strict conditions.

A charged juvenile refused bail must be moved to local authority accommodation unless that is impracticable or, for a juvenile of 12 or over, no secure local authority accommodation is available and other accommodation would not protect the public from serious harm.

episodes.title: Tort WS01 · Revision · 13 min
recap: Personal injury, property damage and consequential economic loss are recoverable in the ordinary way; pure economic loss and psychiatric harm need their special rules.

Apply precedent in an established duty situation and Caparo only in a genuinely novel one; either way, the claimant (or her class) must be reasonably foreseeable as likely to be harmed; a manufacturer of products sold in a form showing that they are intended to reach the ultimate consumer in the form in which they left him, with no reasonable possibility of intermediate examination, owes the consumer a duty to take reasonable care in their preparation, knowing that lack of care may cause injury to life or property; and a duty is owed to a rescuer.
No duty for a pure omission unless D made matters worse or an exception applies, such as assumed responsibility.

No duty to prevent a third party deliberately harming C unless an exception applies; an occupier owes a measured duty for dangers created on its land by trespassers or nature only where it knew or ought to have known of the danger and could reasonably have abated it.
Public bodies owe the same duties as private persons; statutory powers alone create no duty to protect.

episodes.title: BLP WS10 · Trading and voidable transactions
recap: Fraudulent trading: anyone knowingly party to it can be ordered to contribute, not only directors; dishonesty is judged in two steps, what he actually knew or believed and then the standard of ordinary decent people; only the liquidator or administrator can bring the claim, or assign it.

Wrongful trading: a director, shadow directors included, may be ordered to contribute if he knew or ought to have concluded that there was no reasonable prospect of avoiding insolvent liquidation or administration; the only defence is having taken every step to minimise potential loss to creditors that he ought to have taken, and the honest-and-reasonable relief is not available.

Undervalues and section 423: an undervalue needs value, timing and inability to pay debts, with a good-faith defence; section 423 needs a real purpose, with no look-back period and no need for insolvency.

Preferences and floating charges: connection changes the period (except for undervalues, always 2 years) and reverses the burden of proof; a floating charge stays valid to the extent of new value given at the same time or after.

episodes.title: Dispute Resolution WS10 · Jurisdiction and Conflict of Laws
recap: Jurisdiction (can the English court hear it) and applicable law (whose law decides it) are separate questions; foreign law must be pleaded and proved, while procedure and evidence follow English law.

A contract term giving the English courts jurisdiction, exclusive or not, lets you serve abroad without permission, but a governing-law clause alone does not; an exclusive foreign clause normally means a stay, and the Hague Convention makes the stay mandatory, subject to limited exceptions.

Serving a defendant in England and Wales, even briefly, gives jurisdiction as of right, subject to a forum non conveniens challenge; otherwise you need a ground to serve out without permission, or permission, which needs a good arguable case on a gateway, a serious issue to be tried, and England as the proper place.

Serving abroad needs permission unless a ground applies, in which case you file a notice of the grounds; service must be within 6 months of issue, by a method not contrary to the law of the country of service.

Alternative service needs a good reason, and more than that where a service convention applies; it cannot get round the strict rule on extending time, and dispensing with service needs exceptional circumstances.

To dispute jurisdiction, acknowledge service, then apply under Part 11, with evidence, within 14 days after filing the acknowledgment; if you do not, you are treated as accepting jurisdiction, and a step inconsistent with the challenge may amount to submission.

Service in Scotland or Northern Ireland needs no permission only if all three conditions are met: power under the 1982 Act, no pending proceedings on the same claim elsewhere in the UK, and a UK-domiciled defendant (or one of the two special cases).

For a contract, the chosen law governs, subject to three limits; without a choice, the special rules and the type of contract decide, then the characteristic performer's habitual residence, unless the contract is manifestly more closely connected with another country.

For a tort, a valid choice comes first, then the law of the country of common habitual residence, then the law of the country where the damage occurs, unless the tort is manifestly more closely connected with another country; defamation and privacy claims sit outside Rome II.

episodes.title: Property Practice workshop 10 · Lease Termination
recap: If the 1954 Act protects the tenancy, it continues after the contractual term until it is ended under the Act; if not, a tenant who stays on paying rent the landlord accepts may become a periodic tenant, but if a new lease is still being negotiated a tenancy at will is more likely.
Even after its break, a landlord can end a protected tenancy only by a section 25 notice, forfeiture or accepting a surrender.

A periodic tenancy not protected by the Act ends by a notice to quit of the right length, expiring at the end of a period; if the Act protects it, a landlord's notice to quit is ineffective and a section 25 notice is needed.

A landlord can end even a protected tenancy by accepting a surrender, but an agreement to surrender it in advance is void unless the contracting-out procedure is followed; an immediate surrender by deed, with no prior binding agreement, needs no procedure.

In equity, merger turns on intention, so a tenant who shows it intends to keep the lease alive prevents merger; a protected tenant who stays on defeats expiry and a landlord's notice to quit, because the tenancy continues on the same terms until it is ended under the Act.

Rent arrears are recoverable as a debt for 6 years from each payment falling due; against a former tenant or a former tenant's guarantor, only if a section 17 notice was served within 6 months of the sum falling due.

A guarantor of a tenant of a new lease is released when the tenant is released on lawful assignment; recovery from the guarantor of a former tenant needs a section 17 notice within 6 months; a rent deposit lets the landlord draw on it for arrears without court proceedings.

CRAR recovers only principal rent, with VAT and interest on it; at least 7 days' rent must be unpaid both when notice of enforcement is given and when goods are taken, and the notice must be at least 14 clear days before goods are taken, since 1 May 2026.

A tenant can get specific performance of the landlord's repairing covenant, but a landlord gets it against a tenant only exceptionally; a keep-open covenant brings damages, not an order; and an injunction restrains a breach of a negative covenant.

For non-payment of rent, no section 146 notice is needed, but a formal demand is, unless the lease dispenses with it; any other breach needs a section 146 notice and a reasonable time to remedy before re-entry.

Relief for rent arrears is generous, and which route applies depends on whether the landlord forfeited in the county court, in the High Court or by peaceable re-entry, and on when the tenant pays all the arrears and costs.

For a repairing covenant in a lease granted for 7 years or more with 3 years or more unexpired, the section 146 notice must tell the tenant of its right to serve a counter-notice within 28 days, and if it does, the landlord needs leave of the court to forfeit or claim damages.
First ask whether the landlord wants to keep the lease, because forfeiture ends it, subject to relief.

A term granted "from" a date excludes that day and ends on the anniversary; "from and including" a date includes it and ends the day before the anniversary; this is a presumption that clear wording in the lease can displace.

Surrender or merger of the head lease leaves the underlease in place, the undertenant holding directly from the landlord above on the underlease terms; forfeiture ends it, but the undertenant may apply for relief, and the court may vest the premises in it for a term no longer than its underlease.

episodes.title: Tort WS03 · Revision · 17 min
recap: Work in order: factual causation, normally by the but for test, then several causes or tortfeasors, then whether a later event broke the chain.
Causation is all or nothing: a greater than 50% probability establishes it in full, and anything less fails the claim entirely.

A more than negligible contribution to cumulative indivisible harm that science can't apportion means liability in full; mesothelioma needs a material increase in risk; a lost medical chance isn't recoverable.

Each tortfeasor causing the same indivisible damage is liable for the whole, and contribution settles shares; a later tort leaves the first liable for the continuing loss, but a later unrelated natural illness reduces it from that point.
The claimant's own conduct breaks the chain only if so unreasonable that it eclipses the defendant's wrong, and then the later claim fails entirely; mere carelessness only reduces damages.

episodes.title: Tort WS08 · Revision · 19 min
recap: Someone with a proprietary interest or exclusive possession can sue for substantial indirect interference, judged by locality unless physical damage, from a use that is not a common and ordinary use of land conveniently done; personal injury isn't recoverable.

Prescription needs 20 years' enjoyment as of right of an actionable nuisance; coming to the nuisance, public benefit and planning permission are no defences; an injunction is primary but discretionary, so damages may replace it.
In public nuisance an individual needs special damage beyond the public's, but no interest in land, and can recover personal injury and economic loss.
Rylands is strict liability for escapes of dangerous things in non-natural use, but only someone with an interest in the land affected can sue, and only for land or property damage.
